cards.question: Write complete propane combustion with state symbols for hot gaseous products.
Explain why an alkane fuel can require ignition even though combustion is exothermic.
cards.answer: Energy is needed to overcome the activation barrier before reaction proceeds; overall product-bond formation then releases more energy than reactant-bond breaking requires.

cards.question: State one greenhouse gas produced by complete combustion of an alkane.
cards.answer: Carbon dioxide, CO2.

cards.question: Suggest why reduced CO after catalytic exhaust treatment does not prove reduced CO2 production.
cards.answer: The catalyst can oxidise CO to CO2, so lowering CO can increase conversion of exhaust carbon to CO2.

cards.question: State how an infrared monitor can identify a suitable gaseous pollutant.
cards.answer: It detects characteristic absorption bands of that gas.

cards.question: Explain why gas concentration cannot be inferred from absorption strength without controlled optical settings.
cards.answer: Absorption also depends on the optical path and interfering gases, so matched path length and an appropriate calibration are needed to relate signal to concentration.

cards.question: Identify the general composition of a saturated open-chain monohalogenoalkane.
cards.answer: CnH2n+1X, where X is a halogen.

cards.question: Draw displayed bromoethane.
cards.answer: Draw C–C with three explicit H bonds at the first carbon and two explicit H plus Br at the second. C–Br is single; see assets/8224-bromoethane-displayed.png.

cards.question: Name BrCH2CH2CH2Cl.
cards.answer: 1-bromo-3-chloropropane.

cards.question: Suggest the correct name for BrCH2CH2Br.
cards.answer: 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.question: State how each halogen replacement changes the hydrogen count of an otherwise saturated open-chain alkane skeleton.
cards.answer: Each halogen replaces one hydrogen.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of CH3CHBrCH2Cl.
cards.answer: C3H6BrCl.

cards.question: Describe the products formed when bromoethane reacts separately with heated aqueous hydroxide, ethanolic cyanide and excess ethanolic ammonia.
cards.answer: Ethanol by hydroxide substitution; propanenitrile by cyanide substitution with one extra carbon; ethanamine favoured with excess ammonia, alongside ammonium bromide in the net balance.

cards.question: Explain the electron-pair movements when heated aqueous hydroxide substitutes bromine in bromoethane.
cards.answer: An oxygen lone pair forms a bond to the carbon attached to Br while C–Br transfers its pair to Br, giving ethanol and Br− in one step. There is no discrete carbocation intermediate in this direct primary route.

cards.question: Draw the full curved arrows for substitution of bromoethane by heated aqueous hydroxide.
cards.answer: Draw a hydroxide lone-pair arrow to the carbon bearing Br and an arrow from C–Br to Br; products CH3CH2OH and Br−. Both arrows represent pairs in the same step; see assets/8224-bromoethane-hydroxide.png.

cards.question: State the hydrolysis reactivity order for analogous fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes under matched settings.
cards.answer: Fluoro < chloro < bromo < iodo in increasing reactivity.

cards.question: Determine which analogous compound hydrolyses fastest if equal endpoints occur at 150 s for chloroethane, 45 s for bromoethane and 12 s for iodoethane under identical settings.
cards.answer: Iodoethane: it reaches the equal endpoint in the shortest time.

cards.question: Describe how relative inertness supported historical refrigerant and propellant uses of fluorohalogenoalkanes.
cards.answer: Chemical resistance reduced unwanted reactions during service; strong C–F bonding contributed to that resistance; suitable physical properties such as volatility also supported the use.

cards.question: Explain why a strong C–F bond does not prevent ozone-depleting chlorine release from a chlorofluoroalkane.
cards.answer: The molecule can contain a separate C–Cl bond that undergoes stratospheric ultraviolet cleavage; resistance of C–F does not establish resistance of C–Cl under that setting.

cards.question: State the atmospheric consequence of chlorine radicals released from CFCs in the stratosphere.
cards.answer: They catalyse ozone destruction and reduce the protective ozone concentration.

cards.question: Suggest why one stratospheric chlorine radical can participate in destroying multiple ozone molecules.
cards.answer: It is regenerated in the catalytic reaction cycle.

cards.question: State one structural approach used in developing replacements for ozone-depleting chlorofluoroalkanes.
cards.answer: Use a suitable compound without chlorine, removing its C–Cl source of chlorine radicals.

cards.question: Suggest why a chlorine-free replacement cannot be judged environmentally harmless from that fact alone.
cards.answer: It may still absorb infrared radiation and contribute to warming; ozone depletion and greenhouse impact are separate properties.

cards.question: Describe bond energy, bond length and bond polarity.
cards.answer: Bond energy is the energy to break one mole of specified gaseous bonds; bond length is internuclear separation; polarity is unequal sharing of bond electron density.

cards.question: Contrast C–F and C–I when explaining hydrolysis of analogous halogenoalkanes under matched settings.
cards.answer: C–F is shorter, stronger and more polar; C–I is longer, weaker and less polar. Easier C–I cleavage supports faster hydrolysis, showing that polarity alone does not determine rate.

cards.question: Identify the general composition of an open-chain saturated monohydric alcohol.
cards.answer: CnH2n+2O, equivalently CnH2n+1OH.

cards.question: Draw displayed ethanol, including its hydroxyl hydrogen.
cards.answer: Draw C–C–O–H with three explicit H attachments on the first C and two on the second. Each C has four bonds and O has two. See assets/8224-ethanol-displayed.png.

cards.question: Name CH3CH2CH2OH.
cards.answer: Propan-1-ol.

cards.question: Suggest the correct name for CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3.
cards.answer: Butan-2-ol.

cards.question: State whether the hydroxyl hydrogen is included in an alcohol molecular atom count.
cards.answer: Yes; the H bonded to oxygen is part of the total.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of (CH3)3COH.
cards.answer: C4H10O: nine methyl hydrogens plus one O–H hydrogen.

cards.question: Describe ethanol reactions giving ethene, an aldehyde and an ester.
cards.answer: Heated concentrated sulfuric acid dehydrates it to ethene; controlled acidified-dichromate oxidation with product removal gives ethanal; heating with a carboxylic acid and an acid catalyst gives an ester reversibly at fixed temperature.

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for ethanol reacting with sodium.
cards.answer: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2O−Na+ + H2.

cards.question: Write the organic equation using [O] for complete oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid by excess warm acidified dichromate under reflux.
cards.answer: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O. Excess warm acidified dichromate(VI), reflux.

cards.question: Explain why removal of ethanal as it forms helps controlled ethanol oxidation stop at the aldehyde.
cards.answer: Removing the volatile aldehyde reduces its continued contact with the oxidant, limiting further oxidation to ethanoic acid.

cards.question: Explain why “dilute sulfuric acid” does not specify the conventional acid dehydration of ethanol to ethene.
cards.answer: The specified preparation uses concentrated sulfuric acid with strong heating, around170°C. Dilute aqueous acid does not provide that concentrated-acid dehydration setting; concentration and heating must accompany the named reagent.

cards.question: State what is counted when an alcohol is called secondary.
cards.answer: Two carbon groups directly attached to the OH-bearing carbon.

cards.question: Explain why (CH3)2CHCH2OH is primary even though its chain is branched.
cards.answer: The OH-bearing CH2 touches one other carbon, so the local class is primary; branching on a neighbouring carbon does not change that count.

cards.question: Describe the mild oxidation outcomes of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
cards.answer: A primary alcohol can give an aldehyde then acid; a secondary alcohol gives a ketone; a tertiary alcohol resists the ordinary mild route because its OH-bearing carbon has no H.

cards.question: Contrast propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol under controlled oxidation with product identification.
cards.answer: Both reduce warm acidified dichromate from orange towards green. Propan-1-ol gives propanal under controlled product removal, while propan-2-ol gives propanone; colour change alone does not distinguish them.

cards.question: State the positive observation when a suitable alcohol is warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine.
cards.answer: A yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, CHI3.

cards.question: Determine which of propan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol has the alcohol arrangement giving a positive warm alkaline iodine test.
cards.answer: Propan-2-ol: CH3CH(OH)CH3 contains CH3CH(OH)–. Pentan-3-ol lacks the directly attached methyl group.

cards.question: Explain why “the solution turns yellow” is insufficient evidence of a positive warm alkaline iodine test on an alcohol.
cards.answer: A positive result requires a yellow solid precipitate of CHI3, so a solution colour alone does not establish the diagnostic product.

cards.question: Explain why the yellow solid from butan-2-ol and warm alkaline aqueous iodine is not iodobutane.
cards.answer: The test yields triiodomethane, CHI3, a one-carbon precipitate; it is an oxidation/cleavage test of the local arrangement rather than simple replacement of the alcohol OH by iodine on the intact chain.

cards.question: Describe three molecular features relevant to alcohol solvent behaviour.
cards.answer: Polar OH can hydrogen-bond; the hydrocarbon portion interacts with less polar solutes; the balance changes with carbon-chain size, affecting which solutes and water mixtures are compatible.

cards.question: Explain why an alcohol solvent can dissolve some organic ingredients that dissolve poorly in water.
cards.answer: Its hydrocarbon portion provides compatible interactions with less polar parts of the solute while OH supports polar/hydrogen-bond interactions; favourable combined interactions can stabilise the dissolved substance.

cards.question: Identify what is held constant when enumerating isomers from a given molecular atom count.
cards.answer: The numbers and types of atoms; different valid arrangements must retain that composition.

cards.question: Draw and name both open-chain alkane structures with composition C4H10.
cards.answer: Butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, and 2-methylpropane, CH3CH(CH3)CH3. Draw all their connections; both have C4H10 and different carbon skeletons.

cards.question: State the difference between structural isomers.
cards.answer: They have the same molecular composition but different atom connectivity.

cards.question: Suggest the structural-isomer category for propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
cards.answer: Positional isomerism: the OH position differs on the same carbon skeleton.

cards.question: Identify the two syllabus divisions of stereoisomerism.
cards.answer: Geometrical cis–trans and optical isomerism.

cards.question: Draw cis and trans but-2-ene.
cards.answer: Draw each C=C carbon with H and CH3. In cis put methyl groups on the same side; in trans on opposite sides. Connectivity stays CH3CH=CHCH3; see assets/8224-cis-trans-butene.png.

cards.question: Describe the structural requirements and origin of cis–trans isomerism in but-2-ene.
cards.answer: C=C restricts relative rotation; each alkene carbon has two different attachments, H and CH3; same-side and opposite-side methyl arrangements therefore remain distinct under ordinary settings.

cards.question: Explain why turning a whole cis-but-2-ene drawing does not produce trans-but-2-ene.
cards.answer: Whole-molecule rotation preserves the same-side methyl relationship. Changing it requires relative rotation about C=C, which disrupts π bonding and has a substantial energy barrier.

cards.question: Identify the four different groups at the chiral centre of butan-2-ol.
cards.answer: H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3 on carbon2.

cards.question: Draw a tetrahedral mirror-image pair for butan-2-ol, marking its chiral centre.
cards.answer: Mark the OH-bearing carbon C*. Attach H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3 with a solid wedge, a hashed bond and two in-plane bonds; reflect the whole arrangement to produce its non-superimposable mirror. See assets/8224-optical-mirror-pair.png.

cards.question: State why propan-2-ol lacks a chiral carbon at its OH-bearing centre.
cards.answer: That carbon has two identical CH3 groups.

cards.question: Suggest which features in CH3CH=CHCH(OH)CH2CH3 permit the two kinds of isomerism taught here.
cards.answer: Each C=C carbon has H and a different carbon group, permitting geometrical alternatives; the OH-bearing carbon has four different groups and is a chiral centre.

cards.question: Identify the group distinguishing an aldehyde from a ketone.
cards.answer: An aldehyde has at least one H attached to its C=O carbon; a ketone has two carbon groups attached there.

cards.question: Draw displayed ethanal, showing the aldehyde hydrogen.
cards.answer: Draw CH3–C(=O)–H with all three methyl C–H bonds explicit, a C–C single bond, C=O double bond and carbonyl C–H single bond. Oxygen has no O–H bond.

cards.question: Name CH3COCH2CH2CH3.
cards.answer: Pentan-2-one.

cards.question: Suggest the correct name for CH3CH2CH2CHO.
cards.answer: Butanal; include the CHO carbon in the four-carbon parent.

cards.question: State the general composition for saturated open-chain aldehydes and ketones with one carbonyl and no other functional group.
cards.answer: CnH2nO.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of CH3CH2COCH2CH3.
cards.answer: C5H10O.

cards.question: State the reagent used to oxidise a primary or secondary alcohol to a carbonyl in the stated syllabus preparation.
cards.answer: Acidified dichromate(VI), Cr2O7²−/H+, with suitable warming.

cards.question: Suggest how to limit further oxidation when preparing ethanal from ethanol with acidified dichromate(VI).
cards.answer: Use controlled oxidation and distil off volatile ethanal as it forms, reducing its continued exposure to the oxidant.

cards.question: Identify the functional group of a carboxylic acid.
cards.answer: –C(=O)OH, the carboxyl group.

cards.question: Draw displayed methanoic acid.
cards.answer: Draw H–C(=O)–O–H: the carbonyl carbon has a C–H bond, a C=O double bond and a C–O single bond; the second oxygen bears H.

cards.question: Name CH3CH2CH2COOH.
cards.answer: Butanoic acid.

cards.question: Suggest the correct name for (CH3)2CHCOOH.
cards.answer: 2-methylpropanoic acid.

cards.question: State whether the carboxyl carbon is included in an acid molecular atom count.
cards.answer: Yes, along with both oxygens and the O–H hydrogen.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of CH3CH2CH2COOH.
cards.answer: C4H8O2.

cards.question: State which alcohol class can oxidise through an aldehyde to a same-carbon-skeleton acid.
cards.answer: Primary alcohols, using a suitable oxidant.

cards.question: Suggest settings to prepare ethanoic acid from ethanol using acidified dichromate(VI).
cards.answer: Heat under reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI) to favour continued oxidation to the acid.

cards.question: Describe ethanoic-acid reactions with magnesium, sodium hydroxide and sodium carbonate.
cards.answer: Mg gives magnesium ethanoate and H2; NaOH gives sodium ethanoate and water; Na2CO3 gives sodium ethanoate, water and CO2.

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for ethanoic acid reacting with sodium carbonate.
cards.answer: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2.

cards.question: Explain why heating equimolar methanol and ethanoic acid with an acid catalyst does not guarantee complete ester formation at fixed temperature.
cards.answer: Esterification is reversible and reaches an equilibrium containing reactants and products; the catalyst changes rate, not the equilibrium position at that temperature.

cards.question: Identify the group pattern of a neutral primary amine.
cards.answer: RNH2, with one carbon group attached to nitrogen.

cards.question: Draw the ester connection in methyl ethanoate and the primary-amine connection in ethanamine.
cards.answer: CH3–C(=O)–O–CH3 and CH3–CH2–NH2, respectively; show both oxygens in the ester and two N–H bonds in the amine.

cards.question: Name CH3CH2COOCH3.
cards.answer: Methyl propanoate.

cards.question: Suggest the syllabus amino-prefix name for CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3.
cards.answer: 2-aminobutane; it is a primary amine because nitrogen has one carbon attachment.

cards.question: Identify the molecular composition of CH3CH2NH2.
cards.answer: C2H7N.

cards.question: Draw a labelled expansion of CH3COOCH2CH3 and record its molecular atom count.
cards.answer: CH3–C(=O)–O–CH2–CH3; tally four C, eight H and two O, giving C4H8O2. The carbonyl carbon carries no H and neither ester oxygen has an O–H bond.

cards.question: Identify the acid-derived product immediately after methyl ethanoate hydrolysis in heated aqueous sodium hydroxide.
cards.answer: Sodium ethanoate, CH3COONa, not free ethanoic acid.

cards.question: Draw the organic products from heated dilute-acid hydrolysis of CH3CH2COOCH2CH3.
cards.answer: CH3CH2C(=O)OH and HOCH2CH3, propanoic acid and ethanol. At fixed temperature the acid-catalysed hydrolysis is reversible.

cards.question: Describe properties supporting suitable ester uses as solvents, perfumes and flavourings.
cards.answer: Compatible polar/hydrocarbon interactions can dissolve organic solutes; useful volatility enables evaporation; many simple esters have characteristic pleasant odours, though this is not universal.

cards.question: Explain why volatility can support both a suitable ester solvent and a perfume ingredient.
cards.answer: Evaporation removes solvent after carrying dissolved material, while vapour from an odorous ester reaches the nose; suitability still depends on the particular structure and application.

cards.question: Describe a titration setup before an initial burette reading.
cards.answer: Clamp burette vertically above flask/tile; rinse with intended solution and fill tip without bubbles; remove funnel and read meniscus at eye level.

cards.question: Suggest one check if a gas syringe records less gas than expected.
cards.answer: Check the joints and tubing for leaks before repeating the measurement.

cards.question:
Describe the actions and observation points shown in this diagram.

Three labelled boxes linked by arrows: fresh portion of X, add reagent dropwise and record initial effect, add excess of the same reagent and record final effect.
cards.answer: Take a fresh portion of X; follow the diagram arrow to add reagent dropwise and record the initial effect; then add excess of the same reagent and record whether the precipitate remains or dissolves.

cards.question: Suggest why a fresh portion is required for a second candidate-ion test.
cards.answer: It avoids attributing changes caused by earlier reagents to the new test.

cards.question: Describe three features to record when ammonia is added to a coloured precipitate test.
cards.answer: State precipitate formation and colour; record its change with excess ammonia; state the colour and clarity of any resulting solution.

cards.question: Suggest a useful observation beyond “bubbling occurred” when acid is added to a possible carbonate.
cards.answer: Record a suitable confirmation of CO2, such as the gas turning limewater milky under the specified method.

cards.question: Describe taking and recording a delivered burette volume.
cards.answer: Read the appropriate meniscus at eye level; record initial and final readings to0.05 cm³; subtract initial from final to obtain the titre.

cards.question: Suggest a suitable instrument for transferring a25.00 cm³ titration aliquot.
cards.answer: A calibrated25.00 cm³ volumetric pipette with a filler.

cards.question: Describe how to make repeated indicator endpoints consistent.
cards.answer: Use the same indicator amount and visual criterion; slow to dropwise addition near endpoint while swirling; use a white background and check persistence after mixing.

cards.question: Suggest why two close titres do not establish accuracy.
cards.answer: They can share a systematic reagent or calibration bias even when their scatter is small.

cards.question: Describe deciding how many ion tests to perform from supplied candidate notes.
cards.answer: Find a first test separating outcomes; preserve fresh material for a discriminating follow-up if needed; repeat an ambiguous observation rather than adding unrelated reagents to one tube.

cards.question: Suggest why repeating a shared white-precipitate test cannot alone distinguish Al3+ from Zn2+.
cards.answer: Both candidates can give that outcome; a different excess-solubility comparison is needed.

cards.question: Describe a suitable concentration range design for a rate investigation.
cards.answer: Use a pilot to choose measurable endpoints; use several distinct concentrations across the usable range; keep total volume and other reactants controlled and add repeats to assess scatter.
